MOV.description: Copy data from source to destination. The most fundamental instruction. Does not affect any flags. Source and destination must be the same size.
use_cases: Initializing variables and registers with values
Storing computed results to memory locations
Setting up stack frame pointers (MOV ebp, esp)
MOV.notes: MOV is the most frequently used x86 instruction (~25% of all instructions in typical code). Cannot move between two memory operands directly. For moving between memory locations, use MOV reg, [mem] then MOV [mem2], reg.

MOVZX.description: Move with zero extension. Copies a smaller value to a larger register, filling the upper bits with zeros. Commonly used to load unsigned bytes or words into 32-bit registers.
use_cases: Loading unsigned byte/word from memory into a full register
Converting unsigned 8-bit or 16-bit values to 32-bit for arithmetic
Processing ASCII character data where sign extension would be wrong
Loading palette indices, port numbers, and other unsigned small values
MOVZX.notes: Always use MOVZX (not MOV) when loading unsigned data from smaller memory into a register. Using plain MOV would leave upper bits undefined.

MOVSX.description: Move with sign extension. Copies a smaller value to a larger register, extending the sign bit (bit 7 for bytes, bit 15 for words) into all upper bits.
use_cases: Loading signed bytes from memory (e.g., signed char in C)
Converting signed short to int for arithmetic operations
Processing signed data from network protocols or file formats
MOVSX.notes: Essential for correct signed arithmetic. Without sign extension, a negative byte like 0xFF would become 255 instead of -1.

XCHG.description: Exchange values between two operands. Both operands are swapped simultaneously. When used with the accumulator (EAX), it is smaller encoding.
use_cases: Implementing spinlocks (XCHG with memory is atomic)
Swapping two register values without a temporary register
Implementing mutex and semaphore primitives in OS kernels
Sorting algorithms that need to swap array elements
XCHG.notes: XCHG with a memory operand implicitly locks the bus (has LOCK prefix), making it atomic. This is used for spinlock implementations. However, it is slower than separate MOV instructions for simple register swaps on modern CPUs.

LEA.description: Load Effective Address. Computes the address specified by the source operand (without dereferencing it) and stores the result in the destination register. Does not access memory.
use_cases: Fast arithmetic: LEA eax, [ebx+ecx*4+10] computes ebx+ecx*4+10 without memory access
Common compiler optimization for multiplication by small constants
Computing array element addresses: base + index * element_size + offset
Replacing multiple ADD/SHL instructions with a single LEA
Getting pointer to struct field or array element
LEA.notes: LEA does NOT access memory - it only computes an address. This makes it a powerful arithmetic instruction. For example, LEA eax, [ebx+ebx] is equivalent to ADD eax, ebx but uses different execution units. Compilers use LEA extensively for address calculations and as a fast multiply-add instruction.

MOVBE.description: Move big-endian. Loads or stores data in big-endian byte order, performing byte swapping as part of the move.
use_cases: Reading big-endian data from network packets
Loading big-endian values from file formats (e.g., JPEG, PNG headers)
Converting between little-endian (x86 native) and big-endian byte order
Processing protocol headers in network stack implementations
MOVBE.notes: Available on Intel processors since Nehalem. ARM native byte order is also big-endian in some configurations, making this useful for cross-platform code.

CMOVcc.description: Conditional move. Moves data only if the specified condition is met (based on EFLAGS). Avoids branch misprediction penalties.
CMOVcc.example: CMOVZ eax, ebx  ; move if ZF=1
use_cases: Branchless min/max: CMOVG eax, ebx (eax = max(eax, ebx))
Branchless absolute value: CMOVL eax, ebx (negate if negative)
Compiler-generated code for ternary operators (cond ? a : b)
CMOVcc.notes: CMOVcc instructions are the key to branchless programming. They eliminate branch misprediction penalties in if-else patterns. The source operand is always read from the register, but the destination is only written if the condition is true. Conditions: Z/NZ, C/NC, S/NS, O/NO, P/NP, A/AE/B/BE, G/GE/L/LE.

SETcc.description: Set byte to condition code. Sets the destination byte register to 1 if the condition is true, 0 if false. Used for boolean expressions in compiled code.
use_cases: Computing comparison results for C relational operators
Building truth tables and logical operations
Compiler output for if-conditions stored in variables
SETcc.notes: SETcc is how compilers implement C's comparison operators that return 0 or 1. For example, 'int x = (a > b);' compiles to CMP eax, ebx; SETG al. The result is always 0 or 1 in a byte register.

CBW.description: Convert Byte to Word. Sign-extends AL into AX.
use_cases: Sign-extending a byte result to a word for division (IDIV)
Preparing a signed byte for word-sized arithmetic

CWDE.description: Convert Word to Doubleword. Sign-extends AX into EAX.
use_cases: Sign-extending a 16-bit value to 32-bit for IDIV
Preparing signed word results for 32-bit arithmetic
Interfacing with 16-bit APIs that return word-sized results

CDQ.description: Convert Doubleword to Quadword. Sign-extends EAX into EDX:EAX. Must be called before IDIV to sign-extend the dividend.
use_cases: Must be called before IDIV to sign-extend the dividend into EDX:EAX
Creating a 64-bit signed value from a 32-bit register pair
CDQ.notes: ALWAYS call CDQ before IDIV if you want signed division. If you forget, EDX may contain garbage from a previous MUL, giving wrong results. For unsigned DIV, use XOR edx, edx instead.

CQO.description: Convert Quadword to Octaword (x86-64). Sign-extends RAX into RDX:RAX.
use_cases: Prepares 64-bit dividend for IDIV in x86-64 mode

BSWAP.description: Byte swap. Reverses the byte order of a 32-bit or 64-bit register. Converts between little-endian and big-endian.
use_cases: Converting between little-endian and big-endian byte order
Reading big-endian file format headers on x86
Cryptography algorithms that need byte-level permutation
BSWAP.notes: BSWAP eax reverses bytes: ABCD becomes DCBA. This is the software equivalent of MOVBE but operates on registers only. Used extensively in TCP/IP networking for converting between network byte order (big-endian) and host byte order (little-endian on x86).

MOVSB.description: Move string byte: copy byte from [DS:ESI] to [ES:EDI]. Auto-increments/decrements ESI and EDI based on DF flag.

MOVSW.description: Move string word: copy word from [DS:ESI] to [ES:EDI].

MOVSD.description: Move string dword: copy dword from [DS:ESI] to [ES:EDI]. Most commonly used string move for 32-bit data.
use_cases: High-performance memory copying with REP MOVSD (like optimized memcpy)

STOSB.description: Store string byte: write AL to [ES:EDI].
use_cases: Filling memory with a byte value (like memset)
Initializing buffers to zero with XOR eax,eax; REP STOSB

STOSD.description: Store string dword: write EAX to [ES:EDI].
use_cases: Fast memory fill with 32-bit pattern using REP STOSD
Initializing integer arrays to a specific value
Clearing large memory regions: XOR eax,eax; REP STOSD

LODSB.description: Load string byte: read byte from [DS:ESI] into AL.
use_cases: Reading characters from a string for processing
Loading bytes from a buffer for hashing/checksum algorithms

LODSD.description: Load string dword: read dword from [DS:ESI] into EAX.
use_cases: Loading array elements for processing in a loop
Implementing strcmp: REPZ CMPSB / JNZ not_equal

SCASB.description: Scan string byte: compare AL with [ES:EDI].
use_cases: Finding a character in a string (like strchr): REPNE SCASB
Implementing strlen: XOR al,al; MOV ecx,-1; REPNE SCASB
Searching for null terminators or delimiters

REP.description: Repeat prefix: repeats the following string instruction ECX times.
use_cases: Used with MOVSB, MOVSW, MOVSD, STOSB, STOSD
REP.notes: REP decrements ECX before each iteration and stops when ECX=0. With STOS, it fills memory. With MOVS, it copies memory. Always clear EDI/ESI direction with CLD before using REP on x86.

REPE.description: Repeat while equal (ZF=1). Used with CMPS/SCAS for string comparison.
use_cases: Implementing memcmp: REPE CMPSB compares bytes while they match
Finding the first differing byte between two strings

REPNE.description: Repeat while not equal (ZF=0). Used with SCAS to find a character.
use_cases: Implementing strchr: REPNE SCASB finds first occurrence of AL in string
Implementing strlen: REPNE SCASB with AL=0 finds null terminator

PUSH.description: Push value onto the stack. Decrements ESP by 4 (32-bit) or 8 (64-bit) and stores the value at [ESP].
use_cases: Saving register values before function calls (callee-saved registers)
Passing function arguments (cdecl calling convention pushes right-to-left)
Storing temporary values that exceed available registers
Setting up function parameters before CALL

POP.description: Pop value from the stack. Loads value from [ESP] and increments ESP by 4 (32-bit) or 8 (64-bit).
use_cases: Restoring saved register values after function calls
Retrieving function return values in some calling conventions
Cleaning up stack arguments after cdecl function calls

PUSHF.description: Push EFLAGS register onto the stack.
use_cases: Saving flag state before code that modifies flags
Implementing interrupt handlers that need to preserve flags

POPF.description: Pop EFLAGS register from the stack. Restores all flag values.
use_cases: Restoring flag state after interrupt handling
Flag manipulation by modifying stack values then popping

PUSHA.description: Push all general-purpose registers (EAX, ECX, EDX, EBX, ESP, EBP, ESI, EDI) onto the stack.
use_cases: Saving complete register state in interrupt handlers
Context switching in simple operating systems
Quick save of all registers before complex operations

POPA.description: Pop all general-purpose registers from the stack (reverse order of PUSHA).
use_cases: Restoring complete register state after interrupt handling
Context restoration in simple OS kernels

ENTER.description: Create a stack frame for high-level language procedures. Equivalent to PUSH ebp; MOV ebp, esp; SUB esp, size.
use_cases: Setting up stack frames in C/C++ compiled functions
Creating nested stack frames for Pascal-style nested procedures

LEAVE.description: Destroy a stack frame. Equivalent to MOV esp, ebp; POP ebp.
use_cases: Function epilogue to destroy the stack frame
Complement to ENTER instruction in function cleanup

ADD.description: Add source to destination. dest += src. Affects all arithmetic flags.
use_cases: Calculating array offsets: base + index * size
Building up results in mathematical computations
ADD.notes: ADD is one of the most commonly used arithmetic instructions. CF is set if there is an unsigned overflow (carry out). OF is set if there is a signed overflow. ZF is set if the result is zero. PF reflects parity of the low 8 bits.

SUB.description: Subtract source from destination. dest -= src. Affects all arithmetic flags.
use_cases: Adjusting stack pointer: SUB esp, 8 to allocate local variables

MUL.description: Unsigned multiply: EDX:EAX = EAX * src. The 64-bit result spans two registers.
use_cases: Multiplying unsigned 32-bit values to get 64-bit results
Computing array offsets with large indices

IMUL.description: Signed multiply. Two-operand form: dest = dest * src (truncated to dest size).
use_cases: Multiplying signed integers in general computation
Computing array indices with signed offsets
Scale factor multiplication in graphics transforms
Price and financial calculations with signed values
IMUL.notes: IMUL has three forms: (1) one operand: RDX:RAX = RAX * src, (2) two operand: dest = dest * src, (3) three operand: dest = src1 * src2. The two/three operand forms are most commonly used by compilers because they don't clobber the EDX register.

DIV.description: Unsigned divide: EAX = (EDX:EAX) / src, EDX = remainder. ALWAYS clear EDX first!
use_cases: Dividing unsigned values for averaging calculations
Computing array indices from byte offsets
DIV.notes: CRITICAL: Always XOR edx, edx before DIV to clear the upper 32 bits of the dividend. If EDX >= divisor, you get a divide error exception. Division by zero also causes an exception. DIV is one of the slowest integer instructions (20-40 cycles).

IDIV.description: Signed divide: EAX = (EDX:EAX) / src, EDX = remainder. ALWAYS sign-extend with CDQ first!
use_cases: Dividing signed integers (positive and negative values)
Computing signed quotients in financial calculations
Averaging signed sample values in DSP
IDIV.notes: CRITICAL: Always CDQ before IDIV to sign-extend EAX into EDX:EAX. If you forget, EDX may contain garbage, causing wrong results or division overflow exception. IDIV rounds toward zero (truncation), not toward negative infinity.

INC.description: Increment by 1. Preserves CF (carry flag). All other arithmetic flags are affected.
use_cases: Incrementing loop counters (faster than ADD reg, 1 on old CPUs)
Incrementing counters in performance-critical tight loops
INC.notes: INC preserves CF, which is useful when building multi-word arithmetic (e.g., ADC chains). On modern CPUs, ADD reg, 1 is often equally fast or faster due to better macro-fusion properties with subsequent Jcc instructions.

DEC.notes: Like INC, DEC preserves CF. DEC followed by JNZ is a common loop pattern. On modern CPUs, the flag preservation property can prevent macro-fusion with Jcc, making SUB reg, 1 sometimes preferable.

NEG.description: Two's complement negation: dest = 0 - dest. Sets CF=1 if operand is non-zero.
use_cases: Computing two's complement of a value
Implementing subtraction using addition: SUB a,b = ADD a, NEG(b)
Computing absolute value: CDQ; XOR eax, edx; SUB eax, edx

ADC.description: Add with carry: dest = dest + src + CF. Essential for multi-word arithmetic.
use_cases: Adding 64-bit values on 32-bit CPU: ADD low; ADC high
Adding values larger than register width
Carry-propagating addition chains in big number libraries
ADC.notes: ADC is the cornerstone of multi-word arithmetic. For a 64-bit addition on 32-bit x86: ADD eax, [low]; ADC edx, [high]. The carry from the low 32-bit addition automatically propagates via CF to the high 32-bit addition.

SBB.description: Subtract with borrow: dest = dest - src - CF. Essential for multi-word subtraction.
use_cases: Subtracting 64-bit values on 32-bit CPU: SUB low; SBB high
Multi-precision subtraction for big integer libraries
SBB.notes: SBB is the subtraction counterpart of ADC. For a 64-bit subtraction on 32-bit x86: SUB eax, [low]; SBB edx, [high]. The borrow from the low 32-bit subtraction propagates via CF.

XADD.description: Exchange and Add: temp = dest; dest = dest + src; src = temp. Atomic version available with LOCK prefix.
use_cases: Atomic fetch-and-add patterns in concurrent programming

AAA.description: ASCII Adjust after Addition. Adjusts AL after BCD addition.
use_cases: BCD (Binary-Coded Decimal) arithmetic for financial applications

AAS.description: ASCII Adjust after Subtraction. Adjusts AL after BCD subtraction.

AAM.description: ASCII Adjust after Multiplication. Adjusts AX after BCD multiply.

AAD.description: ASCII Adjust before Division. Adjusts AX before BCD divide.

DAA.description: Decimal Adjust after Addition. Adjusts AL for BCD addition result.

DAS.description: Decimal Adjust after Subtraction. Adjusts AL for BCD subtraction result.

AND.description: Bitwise AND. Clears bits where src has 0, preserves bits where src has 1. CF=OF=0, updates ZF/SF/PF.
use_cases: Masking/extracting specific bits: AND eax, 0xFF extracts low byte
Clearing specific bits (bit masking): AND eax, ~0x10 clears bit 4
Checking if a number is even/odd: AND eax, 1; JZ is_even
Implementing modulo by power of 2: AND eax, (n-1) for mod 2^n
Clearing the upper bits of a register
AND.notes: AND with 0xFF extracts the low byte, AND with 0xF extracts a nibble. AND eax, eax is NOT a no-op - it sets ZF based on whether eax is zero (useful before JE). AND always clears CF and OF.

OR.description: Bitwise OR. Sets bits where src has 1, preserves bits where src has 0. CF=OF=0.
use_cases: Setting specific bits: OR eax, 0x10 sets bit 4
Combining flags or option bits: OR eax, FLAG_A | FLAG_B
Setting up memory protection flags in page tables
Enabling features by OR-ing feature bits
OR.notes: OR always clears CF and OF, which makes TEST (which is AND without storing) and OR both clear CF/OF. OR reg, reg also sets ZF based on whether the register is zero.

XOR.description: Bitwise XOR. Toggles bits where src has 1. CF=OF=0.
use_cases: Fastest way to zero a register: XOR eax, eax (2 bytes, 1 cycle, breaks dependencies)
XOR swap algorithm: XCHG without temporary
XOR.notes: XOR eax, eax is the idiomatic way to zero a register in x86 assembly. It is preferred over MOV eax, 0 because: (1) it is shorter encoding (2 bytes vs 5 bytes), (2) it explicitly breaks register dependency chains on out-of-order CPUs, (3) it sets ZF=1 which can be useful. XOR is its own inverse, making it fundamental in cryptography.

NOT.description: Bitwise NOT (one's complement). Flips all bits. Does NOT affect any flags.
use_cases: Computing bitmask for clearing: NOT mask gives the inverse mask
Creating bit patterns for AND operations
Combined with INC to get two's complement: NOT eax; INC eax = NEG eax

SHL.description: Shift left logical. Fills vacated low bits with zeros. Equivalent to unsigned multiply by 2^count.
use_cases: Fast multiplication by powers of 2: SHL eax, 3 multiplies by 8
Building values bit by bit in serialization
SHL.notes: SHL is the fundamental fast-multiplication instruction. On modern CPUs, SHL by a constant is 1 cycle. SHL by CL takes more. CF receives the last bit shifted out. If count > 31, only count mod 32 matters.

SHR.description: Shift right logical. Fills vacated high bits with zeros. Equivalent to unsigned divide by 2^count.
use_cases: Fast unsigned division by powers of 2: SHR eax, 3 divides by 8
Extracting specific bit fields from a value
Converting a value to unsigned by shifting right
Processing bits from MSB to LSB
SHR.notes: SHR fills with zeros (unsigned division). Use SAR for signed division. SHR eax, 1 is the standard way to get the quotient of unsigned eax / 2. The remainder (eax & 1) can be tested separately.

SAR.description: Shift arithmetic right. Fills vacated high bits with the sign bit (bit 31). Preserves sign for signed division.
use_cases: Fast signed division by powers of 2: SAR eax, 1 divides by 2 preserving sign
Implementing signed integer division by constants
Arithmetic right shift for signed values
SAR.notes: SAR is critical for correct signed division. SHR of -16 (0xFFFFFFF0) by 2 gives 0x3FFFFFFC (huge positive number), but SAR gives 0xFFFFFFFC (-4, correct). The difference is that SAR propagates the sign bit.

SAL.description: Shift arithmetic left. Identical to SHL on all x86 processors.
use_cases: Alias for SHL - they produce identical results on x86

ROL.description: Rotate left. Bits shifted out on the left reappear on the right. CF = new LSB (last bit rotated).
use_cases: Rotating bits within a register without losing any
Swapping byte order within a register: ROL eax, 8

ROR.description: Rotate right. Bits shifted out on the right reappear on the left. CF = new MSB (last bit rotated).
use_cases: Extracting groups of bits from the opposite end

RCL.description: Rotate through carry left. CF is included in the rotation as a 33rd bit.
use_cases: Implementing bit-by-bit rotation for arbitrary sizes
Cryptographic algorithms that incorporate the carry bit

RCR.description: Rotate through carry right. CF is included in the rotation as a 33rd bit.
use_cases: Restoring bit position from carry flag

SHLD.description: Double precision shift left. Shifts dest left by count, filling vacated bits with high bits of src.

SHRD.description: Double precision shift right. Shifts dest right by count, filling vacated bits with low bits of src.

BT.description: Bit Test. Copies the specified bit into CF without modifying the operand.
use_cases: Testing if a specific bit is set in a register or memory
Checking status bits in flags registers
Testing individual bits in bitmaps and bit fields

BTS.description: Bit Test and Set. Copies the specified bit into CF, then sets it to 1.
use_cases: Atomically setting a bit (with LOCK prefix)
Allocating resources from a bitmap allocator

BTR.description: Bit Test and Reset. Copies the specified bit into CF, then clears it to 0.
use_cases: Atomically clearing a bit (with LOCK prefix)
Freeing resources in a bitmap allocator

BTC.description: Bit Test and Complement. Copies the specified bit into CF, then toggles it.
use_cases: Toggling a bit atomically (with LOCK prefix)

BSF.description: Bit Scan Forward. Finds the index of the first set bit (from LSB).
use_cases: Finding the lowest set bit (trailing zero count)
Finding the position of the least significant 1-bit
Computing log2 of a power of 2

BSR.description: Bit Scan Reverse. Finds the index of the highest set bit (from MSB).
use_cases: Finding the highest set bit (finding the bit width)
Finding the most significant bit position
BSR.notes: BSR eax, eax computes floor(log2(eax)) + 1 if eax != 0. This is useful for computing the number of bits needed to represent a value, or for normalizing integers.

POPCNT.description: Population count. Counts the number of set bits (1-bits) in the operand.
POPCNT.affects_flags: ZF CF OF SF PF (undefined in some docs)
use_cases: Hamming weight / population count for error detection codes
Counting set bits in hash functions

LZCNT.description: Leading zero count. Counts the number of leading zero bits.
use_cases: Computing the number of leading zeros (CLZ operation)
Finding the highest power of 2 <= x

TZCNT.description: Trailing zero count. Counts the number of trailing zero bits.
use_cases: Finding the position of the lowest set bit
Bit scanning from the least significant end

CMP.description: Compare: computes op1 - op2 and sets flags without storing the result. The foundation of all conditional branching.
use_cases: Comparing values before conditional jumps (if/else in assembly)
Range checking: CMP eax, 100; JA too_big
CMP.notes: CMP is SUB without storing the result. After CMP a,b: ZF=1 means a==b, CF=1 means a<b (unsigned), SF!=OF means a<b (signed). Every if/else, for, while in C compiles to a CMP followed by a Jcc instruction.

TEST.description: Bitwise AND without storing result. Sets flags based on the AND result. CF=OF=0.
use_cases: Checking if a value is zero: TEST eax, eax; JZ is_zero
Testing specific bits: TEST eax, 0x10; JNZ bit4_set
Checking even/odd: TEST eax, 1; JZ is_even
Checking if multiple flags are set: TEST eax, (FLAG_A | FLAG_B)
Fastest zero-check: compilers use TEST instead of CMP reg, 0
TEST.notes: TEST is preferred over CMP reg, 0 because it is one byte shorter (TEST r/m, r) and has the same effect for zero-checking. TEST al, 0xFF checks if any of the low 8 bits are set.

CMPXCHG.description: Compare and Exchange. Compares AL/AX/EAX with dest; if equal, src is stored in dest; otherwise dest is loaded into AL/AX/EAX.
use_cases: Implementing atomic compare-and-swap (CAS) for lock-free algorithms
Implementing lock-free stacks, queues, and linked lists
CMPXCHG.notes: CMPXCHG is the foundation of all lock-free data structures. With LOCK prefix, it atomically compares and exchanges a memory value. The pattern: MOV eax, expected; LOCK CMPXCHG [mem], new_value; JZ success (ZF=1 means values matched).

CMPXCHG8B.description: Compare and exchange 8 bytes. Compares EDX:EAX with mem64; if equal, ECX:EBX is stored.

JMP.description: Unconditional jump. Transfers control to the target address. Always taken.
use_cases: Implementing else branches: JZ then; JMP end; else:
Tail call optimization: JMP instead of CALL + RET
Jumping to error handling or cleanup code

JE.description: Jump if Equal (ZF=1). Also known as JZ.
use_cases: Checking loop termination: DEC ecx; JNZ loop
Testing zero result: TEST eax, eax; JE is_zero
JE.notes: JE and JZ are the same instruction with different mnemonics. JE is used after CMP for readability. JZ is used after TEST or arithmetic for checking zero.

JNE.description: Jump if Not Equal (ZF=0). Also known as JNZ.
use_cases: Loop continuation: CMP ecx, 0; JNE loop
Not-equal branch: CMP eax, ebx; JNE not_equal
Non-zero check: TEST eax, eax; JNE has_value

JG.description: Jump if Greater (signed). ZF=0 AND SF=OF.
use_cases: Signed greater-than comparison: if (a > b) in C with signed types
Implementing signed max() and sorting comparisons
Signed less-than comparison: if (a < b) in C with signed types
Error checking: CMP eax, -1; JL error

JA.description: Jump if Above (unsigned). CF=0 AND ZF=0.
use_cases: Unsigned greater-than: comparing sizes, lengths, addresses
Buffer overflow checks: CMP index, max_size; JA overflow
Pointer comparison: CMP ptr, end_ptr; JA past_end
JA.notes: Using JA/JB for signed values is a common bug! Always use JG/JL for signed (int), and JA/JB for unsigned (size_t, pointers).

use_cases: Bounds checking: CMP index, length; JB out_of_bounds
Carry check after addition: ADC; JB overflow

JGE.description: Jump if Greater or Equal (signed). SF=OF.

JLE.description: Jump if Less or Equal (signed). ZF=1 OR SF!=OF.

JAE.description: Jump if Above or Equal (unsigned). CF=0.
use_cases: Range checks: CMP offset, size; JAE valid_offset

JBE.description: Jump if Below or Equal (unsigned). CF=1 OR ZF=1.

JS.description: Jump if Sign (SF=1). Result was negative.
use_cases: Checking for negative results: SUB eax, ebx; JS underflow
Error code handling: CMP eax, -1; JS is_error

JNS.description: Jump if Not Sign (SF=0). Result was non-negative.

JO.description: Jump if Overflow (OF=1). Signed overflow occurred.
use_cases: Safety checks in arithmetic: ADD eax, ebx; JO too_big

JP.description: Jump if Parity (PF=1). Even number of set bits in low byte.

LOOP.description: Decrement ECX and jump if ECX != 0. Combined DEC + JNZ.
use_cases: Compact loop construct: MOV ecx, N; loop_top: ... LOOP loop_top
LOOP.notes: LOOP is slower than DEC ecx; JNZ on modern CPUs because it has a complex microcode implementation. Compilers prefer DEC/JNZ. However, LOOP is useful for its compact encoding.

LOOPE.description: Decrement ECX and jump if ECX != 0 AND ZF=1.
use_cases: Scanning for a matching byte in a string
Searching until a condition is met or count exhausted

LOOPNE.description: Decrement ECX and jump if ECX != 0 AND ZF=0.
use_cases: Scanning until a non-matching byte is found
String comparison with early exit on mismatch

CALL.description: Call subroutine. Pushes return address (next instruction) onto stack and jumps to target.
use_cases: Implementing recursion (each CALL adds a stack frame)
Calling API functions and library routines
CALL.notes: CALL is the fundamental instruction for function invocation. It pushes the return address (EIP of the next instruction) onto the stack and jumps to the target. RET pops the return address and jumps back. This push-jump / pop-jump pair is the basis of all procedural programming.

RET.description: Return from subroutine. Pops return address from stack and jumps to it.
use_cases: Returning from interrupt handlers (IRET for full context)
RET.notes: RET n (with immediate) adds n to ESP after popping the return address, used in __cdecl to clean up pushed arguments from the caller's perspective.

IRET.description: Interrupt Return. Pops EIP, CS, and EFLAGS from the stack.
use_cases: Restoring complete processor state after interrupt

INT.description: Software Interrupt. Triggers an interrupt handler identified by the number.
use_cases: System calls: INT 0x80 on Linux (32-bit), INT 0x21 on DOS

INT3.description: Breakpoint interrupt (1 byte encoding). Used by debuggers.

CLD.description: Clear Direction Flag (DF=0). String operations auto-increment ESI/EDI.
use_cases: ALWAYS call CLD before REP MOVS/STOS to ensure forward direction
CLD.notes: Always CLD before using string instructions. If DF is set (from a previous STD), string operations will go backwards, causing subtle bugs.

STD.description: Set Direction Flag (DF=1). String operations auto-decrement ESI/EDI.
use_cases: Copying strings in reverse (right to left) for memmove
Processing arrays from end to beginning

CLI.description: Clear Interrupt Flag (IF=0). Disables maskable hardware interrupts.
use_cases: Disabling interrupts in OS kernel during critical sections
CLI.notes: CLI is a privileged instruction in protected mode. Only kernel code can execute it. Disabling interrupts for too long can cause missed interrupts and system instability.

STI.description: Set Interrupt Flag (IF=1). Enables maskable hardware interrupts.
use_cases: Re-enabling interrupts after critical section in kernel
Initial interrupt setup in boot code
Saving flag state in AH register
Restoring flag state from AH register

IN.description: Read a byte/word/dword from an I/O port into AL/AX/EAX.
use_cases: Reading from hardware ports (keyboard controller at 0x60)
IN.notes: IN is a privileged instruction in protected mode. Direct port I/O is only available to kernel-mode code. User-mode programs must use OS-provided APIs for I/O.

OUT.description: Write AL/AX/EAX to an I/O port.
use_cases: Sending commands to hardware (keyboard, PIC, PIT)
Writing to VGA registers for display control
Writing to serial ports for communication
Programming hardware devices in OS kernels

NOP.description: No Operation. Does nothing, advances EIP by 1 byte (0x90).
use_cases: Padding for alignment (aligning loops to 16-byte boundaries)
Debugging placeholder and code patching space
Delay loops (though volatile NOP timing varies)
NOP.notes: NOP is encoded as 0x90 (XCHG eax, eax - a one-byte no-op). Multi-byte NOPs (NOP 2-9 bytes) are used for alignment padding. NOP sleds are used in buffer overflow exploits.

HLT.description: Halt the processor. Stops instruction execution until an interrupt occurs.
use_cases: Halting the CPU when idle (saves power)
End of idle loop in OS scheduler
HLT.notes: HLT is a privileged instruction. The CPU enters a low-power state and waits for an interrupt. Used in the idle loop of OS schedulers: idle: HLT; JMP idle.

LOCK.description: Lock prefix. Asserts LOCK# signal, making the next instruction atomic.
use_cases: Atomic memory operations for multi-threaded synchronization
Implementing spinlocks: LOCK BTS [lock_var], 0; JC spin
Implementing mutexes, semaphores, and reference counts

CPUID.description: CPU Identification. Returns processor feature information in EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX.
use_cases: Runtime CPU feature detection for optimized code paths

RDTSC.description: Read Time-Stamp Counter. Loads 64-bit cycle count into EDX:EAX.

MOVSXD.description: Move with sign-extension from 32-bit to 64-bit (x86-64 only).
use_cases: Sign-extending 32-bit values to 64-bit in x86-64 mode

MOV.description: Move value to register. Can move between registers or load immediates.
MOV.notes: ARM MOV can encode any 16-bit immediate with optional rotation, unlike x86 MOV which can encode 32-bit immediates.

MOVZ.description: Move with zero. Loads a 16-bit immediate into a register, zeroing the upper bits.

MOVK.description: Move with keep. Inserts a 16-bit immediate into a register, keeping other bits.
use_cases: Building large constants: MOVZ + MOVK sequence
Setting specific 16-bit fields of a register

ADD.description: Add two registers or register and immediate.
ADD.syntax: ADD Rd, Rn, Rm / ADD Rd, Rn, #imm

EOR.example: EOR X0, X0, X0  ; zero register

LSL.description: Logical Shift Left. Equivalent to unsigned multiply by 2^n.

LSR.description: Logical Shift Right. Fills with zeros.
use_cases: Fast unsigned division by powers of 2

ASR.description: Arithmetic Shift Right. Preserves sign bit.

CMP.description: Compare: sets flags based on Rn - Rm without storing.

CSEL.description: Conditional Select: Rd = cond ? Rn : Rm.
CSEL.example: CSEL X0, X1, X2, GE  ; max(x1,x2)
CSEL.notes: CSEL is ARM's equivalent of x86 CMOVcc. It selects between two registers based on condition flags, avoiding branch misprediction.

LDR.description: Load Register: loads a word/dword from memory into a register.
LDR.syntax: LDR Rd, [Rn, #offset] / LDR Rd, [Rn, Rm, LSL #scale]

STR.description: Store Register: stores a register value to memory.

LDP.description: Load Pair: loads two registers from consecutive memory locations.
use_cases: Function prologue/epilogue (saving/restoring frame pointer and link register)

STP.description: Store Pair: stores two registers to consecutive memory locations.

LDUR.description: Load Register (unscaled): load with signed byte offset.

BL.description: Branch with Link: saves return address in X30 (LR) and branches.
use_cases: Function calls: BL saves return address in LR

BR.description: Branch to Register: jumps to address in register.

BLR.description: Branch with Link to Register: saves return address and jumps to register.
use_cases: Indirect function calls through function pointers
Zero value branching without separate CMP

CBNZ.description: Compare and Branch if Not Zero.

B.cond.description: Conditional branch based on condition flags.

RET.description: Return: branches to address in X30 (link register).
use_cases: Returning from functions called with BL

SVC.description: Supervisor Call (formerly SWI). Triggers a system call.

MRS.description: Move to Register from System register.

MSR.description: Move from Register to System register.

use_cases: Ensuring all memory accesses complete before proceeding
Flushing the instruction pipeline after self-modifying code
Loading constants (RISC-V has no MOV, use ADDI rd, x0, imm)
Adjusting stack pointer: ADDI sp, sp, -16

SLTU.description: Set Less Than Unsigned: rd = (rs1 < rs2) ? 1 : 0.

XOR.example: XOR x5, x5, x5  ; zero register

XORI.description: Bitwise XOR Immediate: rd = rs1 ^ imm.
use_cases: Computing bitwise NOT: XORI rd, rs1, -1

ORI.description: Bitwise OR Immediate: rd = rs1 | imm.

ANDI.description: Bitwise AND Immediate: rd = rs1 & imm.

SLL.description: Shift Left Logical: rd = rs1 << rs2.

SRL.description: Shift Right Logical: rd = rs1 >> rs2 (unsigned).
use_cases: Fast unsigned division by powers of 2

SRA.description: Shift Right Arithmetic: rd = rs1 >>> rs2 (signed).
use_cases: Fast signed division by powers of 2

LUI.description: Load Upper Immediate: rd = imm << 12. Loads upper 20 bits.
use_cases: Building 32-bit constants with ADDI for lower 12 bits

AUIPC.description: Add Upper Immediate to PC: rd = PC + (imm << 12).

BEQ.description: Branch if Equal: if (rs1 == rs2) pc += offset.
use_cases: Checking for zero: BEQ rs, x0, label

BGEU.description: Branch if Greater or Equal Unsigned.

JAL.description: Jump and Link: rd = PC+4; PC += offset.
use_cases: Function calls: saves return address in rd (usually ra=x1)

JALR.description: Jump and Link Register: rd = PC+4; PC = rs1 + offset.

NOP.description: No Operation (encoded as ADDI x0, x0, 0).

use_cases: Getting upper 32 bits of signed multiplication

ADD.description: Add: rd = rs + rt. Signed overflow trap.

ADDU.description: Add Unsigned: rd = rs + rt. No overflow trap.
use_cases: Most common addition - no overflow exception

ADDI.description: Add Immediate: rt = rs + imm. Signed overflow trap.

ADDIU.description: Add Immediate Unsigned: rt = rs + imm. No overflow trap.

SUBU.description: Subtract Unsigned: rd = rs - rt. No overflow trap.

DIV.description: Divide: LO = rs / rt, HI = rs % rt (signed).
use_cases: MFLO gets quotient, MFHI gets remainder

SLL.description: Shift Left Logical: rd = rt << shamt.

SRL.description: Shift Right Logical: rd = rt >> shamt.
use_cases: Fast unsigned divide by powers of 2

SRA.description: Shift Right Arithmetic: rd = rt >>> shamt.

SLLV.description: Shift Left Logical Variable: rd = rt << rs.

SRLV.description: Shift Right Logical Variable: rd = rt >> rs.

use_cases: Loading 32-bit values from stack or memory
Storing 32-bit values to stack or memory

BEQ.description: Branch if Equal: if (rs == rt) branch.

BLEZ.description: Branch if Less or Equal to Zero.

JAL.description: Jump and Link: $ra = PC+4; PC = target << 2.
use_cases: Function calls: saves return address in $ra

JALR.description: Jump and Link Register: rd = PC+4; PC = rs.

use_cases: Loading upper 16 bits of a constant

concepts.title: What is Assembly Language?
concepts.content:
What is Assembly Language?

Assembly language is a low-level programming language that provides a direct one-to-one mapping to machine code (binary instructions that the CPU executes). Each assembly instruction typically corresponds to a single machine instruction, giving programmers complete control over the hardware.

Key Characteristics:

  • Hardware-Near: Direct access to CPU registers, memory addresses, and I/O ports
  • Architecture-Specific: x86 assembly differs from ARM, RISC-V, and MIPS assembly
  • Minimal Abstraction: No objects, functions (just labels + CALL), or types
  • Maximum Control: Exact cycle-level control over program execution
  • Extreme Performance: Can optimize beyond what compilers achieve

Why Learn Assembly?

  • Understanding how computers actually work at the lowest level
  • Writing performance-critical code (game engines, DSP, cryptography)
  • Reverse engineering and malware analysis
  • Writing OS kernels, bootloaders, and device drivers
  • Debugging optimized code that you can only see in assembly
  • Understanding compiler output and optimization decisions

concepts.title: CPU Registers
concepts.content:
CPU Registers

Registers are the fastest storage in a computer, located directly inside the CPU. They are the primary workspace for all computation. Accessing a register takes 0-1 cycles, while memory access takes 100+ cycles.

x86 Register Hierarchy:

64-bitLow 32Low 16Low 8High 8Typical Use
RAXEAXAXALAHAccumulator, return values
RBXEBXBXBLBHBase (callee-saved)
RCXECXCXCLCHCounter (LOOP, shifts)
RDXEDXDXDLDHData (I/O, MUL/DIV)
RSIESISISIL-Source index (strings)
RDIEDIDIDIL-Destination index
RBPEBPBPBPL-Base pointer (stack frame)
RSPESPSPSPL-Stack pointer
RIPEIPIP--Instruction pointer (PC)

Special Registers:

  • EFLAGS/RFLAGS: Status flags (ZF, CF, SF, OF, PF, DF, IF)
  • Segment Registers: CS, DS, ES, FS, GS, SS (memory segmentation)
  • Control Registers: CR0-CR4 (page tables, protected mode)
  • Debug Registers: DR0-DR7 (hardware breakpoints)
  • MMX/XMM/YMM/ZMM: SIMD vector registers (SSE, AVX)

concepts.title: The Stack
concepts.content:
The Stack

The stack is a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) data structure that grows downward in memory (from high addresses to low addresses on x86). It is essential for function calls, local variables, and expression evaluation.

Stack Operations:

  • PUSH src: ESP -= 4; [ESP] = src (decrement first, then store)
  • POP dest: dest = [ESP]; ESP += 4 (load first, then increment)

Stack Frame Layout (x86 cdecl):

[High Address]
  | Return Address     | <- Caller's PUSH args
  | Arg 2              | 
  | Arg 1              | 
  | Return Address     | <- CALL pushes this
  | Saved EBP          | <- PUSH EBP (prologue)
  | Local Var 1        | <- SUB ESP, N
  | Local Var 2        | 
  ... ESP points here
[Low Address]

Common Stack Patterns:

  • Save/Restore: PUSH eax; ... code ...; POP eax
  • Function Prologue: PUSH ebp; MOV ebp, esp; SUB esp, N
  • Function Epilogue: MOV esp, ebp; POP ebp; RET
  • cdecl Cleanup: Caller does ADD esp, 4*n after CALL
  • stdcall Cleanup: CALLEE does RET n to clean args

concepts.title: EFLAGS Register
concepts.content:
EFLAGS - Status Flags Register

The EFLAGS register contains individual status flags that reflect the result of arithmetic and logical operations. Conditional jumps read these flags to make decisions.

FlagBitSet When...Used By
ZF6Result is zeroJE/JNE, JZ/JNZ
CF0Unsigned overflow (carry/borrow)JB/JA, ADC/SBB, JC/JNC
SF7Result is negative (bit 31 = 1)JS/JNS, JL/JG
OF11Signed overflow occurredJO/JNO, JL/JG
PF2Even parity of low 8 bitsJP/JNP
AF4BCD carry from bit 3AAA, AAS, DAA, DAS
DF10Direction flag (string ops)CLD/STD, MOVS, STOS
IF9Interrupts enabledCLI/STI, hardware IRQs

Flag Combinations for Jcc:

ConditionSigned/UnsignedFlag TestC Equivalent
JE/JZEitherZF=1==
JNE/JNZEitherZF=0!=
JGSignedZF=0 AND SF=OF>
JLSignedSF!=OF<
JGESignedSF=OF>=
JLESignedZF=1 OR SF!=OF<=
JAUnsignedCF=0 AND ZF=0>
JBUnsignedCF=1<
JAEUnsignedCF=0>=
JBEUnsignedCF=1 OR ZF=1<=

concepts.title: Memory Addressing Modes
concepts.content:
Memory Addressing Modes (x86)

x86 supports several addressing modes for accessing memory operands. The general form is:

[base + index * scale + displacement]

ModeSyntaxExampleUse Case
ImmediateimmMOV eax, 42Loading constants
RegisterregMOV eax, ebxRegister-to-register
Direct[addr]MOV eax, [0x1000]Global/static variables
Register Indirect[reg]MOV eax, [ebx]Pointer dereference
Base + Displacement[reg+disp]MOV eax, [ebp-8]Local variables, struct fields
Base + Index[base+index]MOV eax, [ebx+ecx]2D array access
Base + Index * Scale[base+idx*scale]MOV eax, [ebx+ecx*4]Array of 4-byte elements
Full Form[base+idx*scale+disp]MOV eax, [ebx+ecx*4+8]struct.array[i].field

Scale Values:

  • 1: Byte arrays (char, uint8_t)
  • 2: Word arrays (short, uint16_t)
  • 4: Dword arrays (int, float, uint32_t)
  • 8: Qword arrays (long, double, uint64_t, pointers on x86-64)

concepts.title: Calling Conventions
concepts.content:
Calling Conventions

Calling conventions define how functions receive arguments and return values. They are a contract between the caller and callee that ensures consistent behavior across different compilation units and languages.

x86-64 System V (Linux/macOS):

  • Arguments: RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9 (in order), then stack
  • Return value: RAX
  • Callee-saved: RBX, RBP, R12-R15
  • Caller-saved: RAX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, R8-R11
  • Stack alignment: 16-byte aligned before CALL

x86-64 Windows (Microsoft):

  • Arguments: RCX, RDX, R8, R9, then stack
  • Return value: RAX
  • Callee-saved: RBX, RBP, RDI, RSI, R12-R15
  • Shadow space: 32 bytes always allocated on stack

x86 32-bit cdecl:

  • Arguments: Pushed right-to-left on stack
  • Return value: EAX
  • Cleanup: Caller cleans up stack (ADD esp, 4*n)
  • Callee-saved: EBX, ESI, EDI, EBP

ARM64 (AAPCS64):

  • Arguments: X0-X7
  • Return value: X0
  • Callee-saved: X19-X28, FP (X29), LR (X30)
  • Stack: 16-byte aligned, full-descending

concepts.title: Integer Representation
concepts.content:
How Computers Represent Numbers

Unsigned Integers:

Simple binary representation. 8 bits: 0-255, 16 bits: 0-65535, 32 bits: 0-4,294,967,295.

Signed Integers (Two's Complement):

Two's complement is the universal representation for signed integers:

  • Positive: Same as unsigned (e.g., 5 = 0000...0101)
  • Negative: Invert all bits and add 1 (e.g., -5 = ~5 + 1)
  • Range for 32-bit: -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647
  • MSB (bit 31) is the sign bit: 0 = positive, 1 = negative

Hexadecimal Notation:

Base-16 representation, each digit = 4 bits. Prefix: 0x. Commonly used in assembly.

  • 0x00 = 0, 0x0F = 15, 0x10 = 16, 0xFF = 255
  • 0x80000000 = -2^31 (most negative 32-bit signed)
  • 0xFFFFFFFF = -1 (32-bit signed)

Endianness:

  • Little-endian (x86): Least significant byte first in memory
  • Big-endian (ARM, network): Most significant byte first
  • Example: 0x12345678 stored as [78 56 34 12] (LE) or [12 34 56 78] (BE)

concepts.title: Assemblers and Linking
concepts.content:
From Assembly to Executable

The Build Process:

source.asm --[Assembler]--> object.o --[Linker]--> executable

Popular Assemblers:

AssemblerSyntaxPlatformNotes
NASMIntelCross-platformMost popular, clean syntax
GAS (GNU Assembler)AT&TLinux/macOSDefault with GCC, %prefix registers
MASMIntelWindowsMicrosoft's assembler, rich macros
FASMIntelCross-platformFast, self-hosting
LLVM-MCBothCross-platformPart of LLVM toolchain

Intel vs AT&T Syntax:

FeatureIntelAT&T
Operand orderdest, srcsrc, dest
Size suffixDWORD PTRl (long)
Register prefixeax%eax
Immediate prefix42$42
Dereference[eax](%eax)

Common Assembler Directives:

  • section .text - Code section
  • section .data - Initialized data
  • section .bss - Uninitialized data (zeroed)
  • global/main - Export symbol
  • extern - Import symbol
  • db/dw/dd/dq - Define byte/word/dword/qword data
  • equ - Define constant
  • times - Repeat instruction
  • macro - Define macro

concepts.title: Common Assembly Patterns
concepts.content:
Common Assembly Patterns

If-Else:

CMP eax, ebx
JGE .else
  ; if branch (eax < ebx)
  MOV eax, 0
  JMP .endif
.else:
  ; else branch (eax >= ebx)
  MOV eax, 1
.endif:

For Loop (count up):

MOV ecx, 0      ; i = 0
.loop:
  CMP ecx, 10    ; i < 10
  JGE .done
  ; body: use ecx as i
  INC ecx        ; i++
  JMP .loop
.done:

Function Call (cdecl):

; Caller:
PUSH arg3
PUSH arg2
PUSH arg1
CALL function
ADD esp, 12    ; clean 3 args * 4 bytes
; result in EAX

; Callee:
function:
  PUSH ebp      ; prologue
  MOV ebp, esp
  SUB esp, 8    ; local vars
  ; ... body ...
  MOV esp, ebp  ; epilogue
  POP ebp
  RET

Switch/Case (jump table):

CMP eax, 3
JA .default
JMP [jump_table + eax*4]
jump_table:
  DD .case0
  DD .case1
  DD .case2
